title: UPDATE: Here's another headache for beaten-up auto stocks
text:
By Victor Reklaitis, MarketWatch
Critical information for the U.S. trading day
Americans are falling out of love with their cars -- at least when it comes to the daily commute.
Wolf Richter, of the Wolf Street financial blog, cites this growing challenge for the auto market, in our call of the day.
"Driving, while still by far the top way of getting to work in America, has lost some ground," Richter writes (https://wolfstreet.com/2018/09/02/automakers-take-note-americans-are-changing-how-they-commute-to-work/). "For auto makers, this is not a propitious trend."
Richter has created the chart below that's based on recent Gallup polling (https://news.gallup.com/poll/241805/commuters-work-without-cars-past.aspx). It shows a jump in the percentage of American workers who don't use a car in their commute. That figure climbed to 16% this year, up from 9% in 2007.
Instead of driving themselves or carpooling, these folks are taking public transportation, telecommuting, biking, walking or doing "something else" (maybe going by boat or scooter?).
"This shift is real," Richter says. "While the annual increments are small, spread over time they will further impact the dynamics of the auto industry."
Don't miss:U.S. auto sales maintain momentum for now (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/us-auto-sales-maintain-momentum-for-now-2018-09-04-141032838)
Some 77% of U.S. workers drive themselves, down from 85% in 2007, he adds. "At this rate, the percentage might drop to something like 69% over the next decade."
Shares in Detroit's Big Three have struggled of late. General Motors (GM) , Ford (F) and Fiat Chrysler (FCA.MI) (FCA.MI) have suffered year-to-date losses that range from about 3% to 24%, while the S&P 500 is up around 8%.
The car stocks been whacked by expectations of higher materials costs (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/gm-slammed-by-tariffs-as-steel-and-aluminum-costs-soar-2018-07-25) due to the recent U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum, and the view that the auto industry (CARZ)will suffer from trade tensions more broadly (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/heres-how-much-trumps-threatened-car-tariffs-would-add-to-cost-2018-07-19).

Key market gauges

Europe (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/european-stocks-drop-as-trade-worries-persist-2018-09-05) is losing ground, with analysts yet again blaming the selling on global trade tensions. Asian gauges fell sharply, (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/asian-stocks-a-bit-of-a-mess-with-widespread-declines-2018-09-04) as fears about emerging-markets crises continued to weigh. Oil is lower, while gold and the dollar index are trading flat to slightly higher. Bitcoin is changing hands around $7,400.

(http://www.marketwatch.com/story/workday-stock-declines-as-earnings-miss-drags-on-raised-outlook-2018-09-04)Tesla's (TSLA) Elon Musk has doubled down (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/elon-musk-doubles-down-on-personal-attack-against-cave-rescuer-calls-him-child-rapist-2018-09-04) on his personal attack on a British cave-diving expert.
The companies on the earnings docket ahead of the opening bell include Vera Bradley (VRA) , the accessories seller whose stock has rallied (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/vera-bradley-shares-jump-86-after-losses-narrow-guidance-raised-2018-06-06) about 60% over the past 12 months. After the market's close, watch for results from drones maker AeroVironment (AVAV) and a few software companies -- DocuSign (DOCU) , Guidewire (GWRE) and Cloudera (CLDR) .
On the Federal Reserve front, the St. Louis Fed's James Bullard is due to talk before the open, and the New York Fed's John Williams is expected to make multiple appearances (https://www.newyorkfed.org/newsevents/mediaadvisory/2018/0822-2018) in upstate NY today and tomorrow. After the closing bell, the Minneapolis Fed's Neel Kashkari and the Atlanta Fed's Raphael Bostic are slated to make remarks.
British prosecutors have charged two Russian men (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/uk-charges-two-russians-with-attempted-murder-of-spy-daughter-2018-09-05-61034226) with attempting to murder a spy and his daughter in Salisbury in March.

The incendiary tell-all book by the reporter who helped bring down President Nixon has put the White House in damage-control mode, says an AP report (https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/articles/2018-09-04/woodward-book-says-trump-aide-privately-called-him-idiot).
The chart
"If we look at the FAANGM stocks (Facebook (FB) , Apple (AAPL) , Amazon (AMZN) , Netflix (NFLX) , Google (GOOGL)(GOOGL) , Microsoft (MSFT) ), and plot their number of employees versus their annual revenues over their lifetimes (on a log-log chart) we would see a striking relationship," says Ritholtz Wealth Management's Nick Maggiulli, as he does exactly that with his chart shown above.
"Every time the number of employees doubles (a 100% increase), revenue goes up by 112% (more than double)," writes Maggiulli in a blog post (https://ofdollarsanddata.com/what-will-always-be-true/) that has been getting attention.
Check out:Amazon briefly crosses $1 trillion market-cap mark (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/amazon-briefly-crosses-1-trillion-market-cap-mark-2018-09-04)
Ritholtz Wealth's analytics manager adds: "What's even more amazing is that this relationship holds across all of these individual companies despite their different business models and hiring practices."
